The main feature of the intelligence of the past week is the interruption of peace and good order thr ugh everv s iciety in Europe, our own not cxcerted : this is a natural consequence of the French ltevoluti > , which, I'kc ho memoVablc earthquake oi Lisbon in tne days of our grandfathers, tins communion ted its shock, in a greater or less degree, to all iis neighbours, near rod remote. Happily, however, though (he surface of tire waters is almost universally heaved up and broken in the other kingdoms of Europe, what are waves and billows in those nations, arc lit lie more in our own than mere bubbles, which break and disappear almost as soon as they rise. The fortunate truth is, that there is nothing so absolutely powerless, except indeed for small mischief, as an English town mob, wholly unarmed, and unskilled in the use of arms, impelled by a blind and ignorant folly, and unaided by the sympathy of any class above themþÿ regarded by the police with anger, by the military with derision, and by every householder with dislike and disgust þÿ in a Word, considered only as a collection of 'vagabonds, whom it is the common interest to disperse and to correct. In France things are wholly different. The mobs are there composed of discharged soldiers. A very large proportion of the persons in the recent insurrection had been formed by military training and exercise; they knew the use of arms, and could raise

barricades and earth works; they could conrcit even thing into a pike, and could make the best of it ; they manifested some union and joint momentum in their attack, and were steady and S' If collected in their de fence. The National Guards and the trades freely mixed with them: and in the late political conflict, one of the great parlies adopted and covertly encouraged them, go that a large portion of public opinion rallied around tlicin This was caught bv the soldiery and their officers. Indeed, it had hecorhe a matter of peril to the goldierv to proceed with «oo much vigour and severity against them. But m England there is nothing of this kind.

No respectable man lias any other wish end object but to ensure thai quiet of his own dwelling and the safely of his property by the steady dispersion and merited correctional punishment of the rioters. During the past week there have been many scenes of this most senseless and d is graceful rioting,þÿ in our own metropolis, and in Glasgow, Are. But we nowhere meet any person who assigns any lurther consequences to them than of tlieir being so many cursory interruptions of public peace and quiet. It is a matter for the poftce only. When were, the power and functions if the Sovereign more entirely and consiituTunuly merged in the responsible minister a of her Gaintret ? Now is the government, or the police, at least, in n proper state and duly administered, if this lie too long allowed t To tie just,

however, we must admit that we have hitherto seen much to commend, and nothing to censure, in the humanity and discretion of the Home Office, and in the moderation and good conduct ol tire police in out own metropolitan mobs up to the present time. We could wish only that more summary commitments were made, and that in the case of

reputed thieves, they were commuted at once to the thiee months' hatd labour allowed by the statute. Commitments without ha:d labour is no punishment to this class of vagabonds. It may he Well imagined, that this turbulent state of England and Europe has added much to the depressed condition of trade and commerce, and has contracted our home consumption as welf as the demand of the foreign market. It has, indeed, Accomplished this to a very great and afflicting excess þÿ not only by that apprehension of futuie consequences' which withhold men from any large and liberal expenditure of their means, but by the absolute and present diminution and cutting off of such means. Every day's post brings an account of the failure of foreign bankers. The great house formerly Lafitte's has stopped payment, and scarcely a week occurs but that Antwerp, Amsterdam, Hamburg, and some other imperial city, adds some new example of the distress of trade and commerce Under such circumstances, we can scarcely express our astonishment at the inconsiderate tashness of the Whig ministers in endeavouring to impose fresh burdens on the people It is our sincere opinion, that the proposed increase of the tnronre tax Would have destioyed the tax itself, if it had been carried through the house. It was entirely by this arm of defence, that Athens, a government whose actual territory did not exceed the extent of an English county, sustained itself for upwards of one hundred years against the vast magnitude of the Persian empire; and afterwards, for upwards of two centuries, against the greater, because better compacted power, of all the Grecian States ur.ited against her. She was only conquered at last by Philip of ftlaeedon, the father of Alexander the Great because his accumulated treasures enabled him to cor rupt her statesmen and orators, and because, in the disturbance and confusion of her finances, she lost the means of supporting her fleet. How great, also, became the power of Venice and Genoa, whilst their opulent and flourishing commerce afforded them the same naval strength ; and in a much later age how nearly equal almost became the Dutch and English nations. All that we mean briefly is, that England, whilst mistress of the seas, possesses the proper, characteristic, and independent power, which, under the blessing of Providence, is fully sufficient for our own defence, and puts us at least above the necessity of seeking our own safety by encumbering omselies with the cost of these interpositions in foreign

quarrels, and of drawing our swords in other þÿ m e n s causes. But an extreme ease of this kind, being then in fact the cause of a Power, whose call to act as It is secondaiy instniment all mankind must at once obey, will, when it arises, become sufficiently indicated by its own circumstances or to speak more plainly, we shall then have no choice ; we shall at once he forced into the path of duty, and it then only remains to do willingly, zealously, and conscientiously, what we then must do at all events. On Sunday afternoon, the Kith inst , between 2 and 3 þÿ o c l o c k , the alarm gun was fired in the Court yatd ol Government house, and repeated by the fort Alexander, in consequence of news having been received of a revolt in the South of the island. The President, with his stalT of General Officers and suit repaired at once to the Arsenal, and thence back o the Palace, on his return he immediately summoned the General of Division Celegney Ardouin (exminister of the interior, under the late President Riche and brother to the Haytien Envoy in Paris) to answer to an accusation of conspiracy against the Government, and ordered him to prison. The Court sard in front of the Government house was gradually lined with troops, and a t umber of black and coloured officers, with many of the lower class of the populace assembled before the door of the Palace. At the moment that Gen. Ardouin surrendered himself to the oidt-rs of the President, he was fired at bv one of die crowd, and fell by a pistol shot, several othei shots were fired, and the troops, it is said, under the impression (fiat the þÿ P r e s i d e n t s life was menaced, discharged a volley ol musketry on those assembled in the doorways of the Palace, which killed a colouted Gen. named Petouches, favourable to the government,

with several soldiers and wounded others. Another coloured man, Cerisior, secretary to the Minister of Foreign Atlairs in attempting to leave w as shot by the troops, most of the O n. Officers and other persons of note who honied from the Palace, were also fired on, Out without receiving much harm The British Consul, Thomas N.
